Header: Phytophthora cinnamomi , P. parasitica Uozo in Swahili, root rot or heart rot in English

Prevention: Avoid growing pineapples in shady, humid areas.
Plant the crop on well drained non-heavy soils, and not in low land.
Raise planting beds at least 23 cm high for settling of the plant.
Between raised beds, build trenches to get rid of excess water without causing soil erosion.
Deep rip down the slope before hilling if soil is compact
Practice plant space of at least 60 cm
Apply phosphorus fertilizers to strengthen plant.
Avoid evening irrigation, as moisture cannot dry on leaves.
Avoid overhead irrigation to minimize splashes.
Avoid flooding or furrow irrigation otherwise disease will be carried over.
Only irrigate from healthy to unhealthy crop areas.
Mulch and re-mulch with any dry plant debris except from pineapples to reduce muddy conditions
Remove pineapple residue after harvest, and leave in sun to reduce disease.
However, if no major insect pests and diseases are in your crop, then leave the residues to improve the soil, and reduce water evaporation.
After heavy rot disease infestation, do not grow pineapples for several years on the same plot.
Monitoring: Root rots, top rots, or heart rots are all watery mould diseases, a bit like fungal diseases.
Start scouting for symptoms two weeks after planting; then every two weeks.
Look for: reddish heart leaves; then light brown with light tinge; then yellowish with necrotic leaf edges.
Curved leaf edges that become limp and die back from tips.
Terminal whorl can easily be pulled from mother plant
Water soaked tissue at base of leaves have a foul smell
If symptoms are seen on 5-7 plants per quarter of an acre, quick action is advised
Direct Control: Rouge out diseased plants and deeply bury them outside the field
WG 66.8, and others); dithiocarbamate group of fungicides, with protective action.

Losses from top and root rots are usually a result of poorly drained soils.
However, tops may also be affected on well-drained soils if long wet weather follows planting.
Only then chemical control options may be advised.
Pineapple rots are not true fungi; therefore most fungicides do not work, except for those listed here.
Use metalaxyl-based products; or products based on a mix of metalxyl and mancoceb (Agrilax 720WP, Eureka 72WP, Mancolax 72%WP, Ridomil
